questions.question: Kennedy was president during the 1963 March on Washington. What was his position on it beforehand?
options: He was abroad and learned of it afterward
He helped plan the route and speaking order
He tried to get organisers to call it off
He addressed the crowd immediately before King
questions.answer: He tried to get organisers to call it off
questions.explanation: Kennedy feared a large demonstration would harden congressional opposition to the civil rights bill and pressed organisers to cancel. They refused, and he then worked to shape it, with the administration arranging a cut-off switch for the sound system in case speeches turned militant. John Lewis was pressured into softening his text. Around 250,000 attended peacefully. Kennedy met the leaders afterward and was assassinated eleven weeks later.
questions.memory_hook: Kennedy tried to get it cancelled, fearing it would harden opposition to his civil rights bill. When organisers refused he worked to manage it, including a kill switch on the sound system in case speeches got militant. John Lewis was pushed to tone his down. He was dead eleven weeks later.

questions.question: The Meiji Restoration ended samurai rule in Japan. What happened to the samurai themselves?
options: They kept full privileges but lost all political power
Their stipends were abolished and swords banned in public
They were exiled to Hokkaido as a separate province
They became the officer corps of the new imperial army
questions.answer: Their stipends were abolished and swords banned in public
questions.explanation: The government converted hereditary stipends into bonds, then banned the wearing of swords in 1876, dismantling both the income and the identity of a class of roughly two million. Some moved into business, bureaucracy and the new conscript army, but many were ruined. Saigo Takamori led the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion in protest and was crushed by peasant conscripts armed with rifles, which settled the question definitively.
questions.memory_hook: Stipends were converted to bonds and then swords were banned in public in 1876, wiping out both the income and identity of about two million people. Saigo Takamori rebelled in 1877 and was destroyed by peasant conscripts with rifles, which rather made the point.

questions.question: Angela Merkel was a scientist before entering politics. What was her field?
options: Quantum chemistry, with a doctorate from East Berlin
Medicine, practising as a paediatrician until 1989
Civil engineering, specialising in bridge design
Economics, advising the East German finance ministry
questions.answer: Quantum chemistry, with a doctorate from East Berlin
questions.explanation: Merkel earned a doctorate in quantum chemistry and worked as a research scientist at the Academy of Sciences in East Berlin until 1989. She entered politics only after the Wall fell, at thirty-five, and became Chancellor sixteen years later. Observers frequently attributed her deliberate, evidence-first decision-making style to that training. She grew up in the GDR as a pastor's daughter and speaks fluent Russian.
questions.memory_hook: She had a doctorate in quantum chemistry and worked as a research scientist in East Berlin until 1989. She only entered politics after the Wall fell, at thirty-five, and was Chancellor sixteen years later. Pastor's daughter, raised in the GDR, fluent Russian.

questions.question: Jesse Owens won four golds at the 1936 Berlin Olympics. What's the truth behind the story that Hitler 'snubbed' him?
options: Hitler hosted him at a state dinner in the Olympic Village
Hitler waved to him; it was FDR who ignored him
Hitler walked out of the stadium and the IOC objected
Hitler skipped every event Owens competed in
questions.answer: Hitler waved to him; it was FDR who ignored him
questions.explanation: The 'Hitler snub' is largely a myth perpetuated by sportswriters. Owens himself said Hitler waved at him and Owens waved back. After the 100m, Hitler sent a signed photograph. Owens told reporters: 'When I passed the Chancellor, he arose, waved his hand at me, and I waved back at him. I think the writers showed bad taste in criticizing the man of the hour in Germany.' Owens was not invited to the White House by FDR (who did celebrate white athletes), and he had to enter his own New York ticker-tape parade reception through a back door. He remarked that Hitler acknowledged him but his own president did not.
questions.memory_hook: Owens himself said Hitler waved and he waved back — and that Hitler had treated him better than FDR did. Roosevelt celebrated the white athletes but didn't invite Owens to the White House. Owens entered his own NYC ticker-tape parade reception through a back door. The 'snub' story was invented by American sportswriters.

questions.question: FIFA governs world soccer and has faced repeated corruption allegations. What happened in 2015?
options: The UN placed formal sanctions on the organisation
US authorities indicted officials, arrested in a Zurich hotel
European federations withdrew from FIFA entirely
FIFA voluntarily dissolved and reformed under a new name
questions.answer: US authorities indicted officials, arrested in a Zurich hotel
questions.explanation: Swiss police acting on US indictments arrested FIFA officials at the Baur au Lac hotel in Zurich in May 2015, walking some out behind bedsheets to shield them from cameras. The charges covered racketeering and wire fraud around media rights worth over $150 million. Sepp Blatter was re-elected days later and resigned within a week. The US had jurisdiction because payments moved through American banks.
questions.memory_hook: Swiss police acting for US prosecutors arrested FIFA officials at a Zurich hotel in 2015, some led out behind bedsheets to hide from cameras. Racketeering and wire fraud over media rights worth $150 million plus. Blatter was re-elected days later and quit within a week.

questions.question: Apocalypse Now (1979) nearly destroyed its director. What went wrong during production?
options: The Philippine government seized the film mid-shoot
The negative was lost in transit and reshot entirely
Financing collapsed and the crew went unpaid for a year
A typhoon, a heart attack, and a lead actor's collapse
questions.answer: A typhoon, a heart attack, and a lead actor's collapse
questions.explanation: A typhoon destroyed the sets, Martin Sheen had a heart attack at thirty-six, Marlon Brando arrived overweight and unprepared having not read the book, and the Philippine helicopters on loan kept leaving to fight an actual insurgency. Coppola mortgaged his own property to finish and later said the film was not about Vietnam, it was Vietnam. The shoot ran 238 days against a planned six weeks.
questions.memory_hook: A typhoon flattened the sets, Sheen had a heart attack at thirty-six, Brando turned up overweight without having read the book, and the borrowed Philippine helicopters kept flying off to fight a real insurgency. Coppola mortgaged his own property. 238 days against a planned six weeks.

questions.question: John Lennon later described Imagine as an anti-religious, anti-nationalist song. Why did it become so widely acceptable?
options: He said the message was sugar-coated enough to slip past
Yoko Ono rewrote the lyrics for the single version
It was only released after his death, stripped of context
Radio stations edited out the more provocative verses
questions.answer: He said the message was sugar-coated enough to slip past
questions.explanation: Lennon acknowledged the song was essentially a political statement made palatable by a gentle melody, and said as much in interviews. It has since been played at Olympic ceremonies, memorials and New Year broadcasts, often by institutions the lyrics argue against. Yoko Ono received a co-writing credit in 2017 after Lennon had long said the concept came from her book Grapefruit.
questions.memory_hook: Lennon admitted it was a political statement sugar-coated by a pretty tune so people would swallow it. It now gets played at Olympic ceremonies and memorials by exactly the institutions it argues against. Yoko Ono got a co-writing credit in 2017, since the idea came from her book.

questions.question: Mark Rothko made 14 near-black paintings for the Rothko Chapel in Houston. What did he intend them to do?
options: Shift in color with the changing light through the day
Overwhelm the viewer with presence in absolute silence
Key each panel to a different faith's sacred text
Serve as unfinished works darkened by his declining health
questions.answer: Overwhelm the viewer with presence in absolute silence
questions.explanation: Rothko accepted the commission from John and Dominique de Menil in 1964 and spent years working on the 14 panels, which are nearly black but contain deep purples and maroons visible as eyes adjust. He designed the lighting, insisted on specific panel arrangements, and saw the chapel as the culmination of his career — wanting viewers to feel 'enveloped' rather than simply looking at paintings. He died by suicide in 1970, a year before the chapel opened. It has become an interfaith pilgrimage site hosting world leaders including Jimmy Carter and the Dalai Lama. Rothko said his paintings were 'about tragedy, ecstasy, doom, and so on.'
questions.memory_hook: Rothko spent years on the 14 near-black panels, dying by suicide in 1970, one year before the chapel opened. The panels appear black at first glance but reveal deep purples and maroons as eyes adjust. He designed the space to envelope rather than be viewed from a distance. It became an interfaith site hosting Carter, the Dalai Lama, and others.

questions.question: The Serengeti hosts the largest land mammal migration on Earth. What actually drives it?
options: A fixed migratory instinct inherited over generations
Rainfall patterns dictating where grass is growing
Predator pressure pushing herds steadily northward
Seasonal drying of the only permanent water source
questions.answer: Rainfall patterns dictating where grass is growing
questions.explanation: Roughly 1.5 million wildebeest plus zebra and gazelle follow rain and the grass it produces in a rough clockwise loop through Tanzania and Kenya. The route shifts year to year with the weather rather than following a fixed path. Around 400,000 calves are born within a few weeks on the short-grass plains, swamping predators so most survive. Crossing the Mara River is the famous and lethal part, with crocodiles and drownings.
questions.memory_hook: About 1.5 million wildebeest plus zebra and gazelle chase rainfall and the grass it brings in a rough clockwise loop, and the route changes yearly with the weather. Some 400,000 calves drop within a few weeks so predators cannot eat them all. The Mara crossing is the part with the crocodiles.

questions.question: What is the name of the boundary between Earth's crust and mantle?
options: Mohorovicic discontinuity
Gutenberg discontinuity
Lehmann discontinuity
Conrad discontinuity
questions.explanation: The Mohorovicic discontinuity (or 'Moho') is the boundary between Earth's crust and upper mantle, located approximately 35 km below the continents and 5-10 km below the ocean floor. It was discovered by Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovicic in 1909 by analyzing seismic wave speeds. Below the Moho, seismic waves travel faster because of the denser mantle rock.
questions.memory_hook: Moho = crust-mantle boundary. Named after Croatian geologist Mohorovicic. Discovered by studying how earthquake waves change speed at this depth. The crust you live on is just the thin surface layer — below it is the mantle where rocks are hot enough to flow over millions of years.

questions.question: The Black Forest gave its name to a famous cake and something else entirely. What?
options: The oldest continuously operating brewery in Europe
The first European ski resort, opened in 1840
Cuckoo clocks, made there since the eighteenth century
Germany's first national park, designated in 1902
questions.answer: Cuckoo clocks, made there since the eighteenth century
questions.explanation: Farming families in the Black Forest built clocks through long winters when field work stopped, and it grew into a major industry, with the cuckoo mechanism becoming the regional signature. The forest is named for its dense dark conifers that block light at ground level. It is also the source of the Danube, and the Brothers Grimm drew on the region's folklore.
questions.memory_hook: Farming families built clocks through the winters when there was no field work, and it became an industry, with the cuckoo as the local signature. The name comes from conifers so dense the forest floor stays dark. The Danube rises there, and the Grimms mined the local folklore.

questions.question: Passing electricity through water splits it into hydrogen and oxygen. Why is this suddenly commercially interesting?
options: Hydrogen made from renewables burns without carbon output
It is the cheapest way to produce drinking water
The oxygen produced is more valuable than the hydrogen
It removes dissolved carbon dioxide from seawater
questions.answer: Hydrogen made from renewables burns without carbon output
questions.explanation: Electrolysis powered by solar or wind produces green hydrogen, which releases only water when burned or used in a fuel cell. It offers a route to decarbonising steel, shipping and fertiliser, which resist direct electrification. Most hydrogen today still comes from natural gas and emits heavily. The obstacles are efficiency losses, since you lose energy converting twice, and the difficulty of storing a molecule small enough to leak through most materials.
questions.memory_hook: Electrolysis run on solar or wind gives green hydrogen, which emits only water, and that matters for steel, shipping and fertiliser, which are hard to electrify directly. Most hydrogen today is still made from natural gas. The catch is you lose energy converting twice, and it leaks through almost everything.
